title: And Then, It All Made Sense
subtitle: A Love Letter to Struggling Students
appreciation: All praise and gratitude belong to Allah, whose mercy, guidance, and favour have brought me this far. Alhamdulillah for every lesson, every answered prayer, and every moment that eventually made sense.

To my mum and dad, thank you for your sacrifices, prayers, love, and unwavering support. To my family, lecturers, mentors, friends, and everyone who contributed to my journey in one way or another, I am deeply grateful.
May Allah reward you all abundantly.
Every journey has a story, and this is a little piece of mine. A story of hope, courage, struggles, and becoming.
And Then, It All Made Sense
author: Roqeebah Olaide Onigbanjo
paragraphs: AND THEN, IT ALL MADE SENSE
A Love Letter to Struggling Students.
By
ONIGBANJO Roqeebah Olaide.
RN, RM, RPHN, BNSc (First Class Honours)
DEDICATION
TO EVERY STRUGGLING STUDENT OUT THERE.
TABLE OF CONTENTS
DEDICATION
To Every Struggling Student Out There
APPRECIATION
To Those Who Walked the Journey with Me
PROLOGUE
Before the Journey Began
CHAPTER ONE
Maybe the Struggle Started Earlier
CHAPTER TWO
When Life Didn’t Go as Planned
CHAPTER THREE
The Third Attempt: Adams College
CHAPTER FOUR
My COVID Season and My Second Return to Adams College
CHAPTER FIVE
My Fifth UTME: Cairo University or Crescent University?
CHAPTER SIX
Gaining Admission into Crescent University.
CHAPTER SEVEN
Transitioning into the Nursing Department
CHAPTER EIGHT
Year Three: The Beginning of My Professional Examinations
CHAPTER NINE
My Second Professional Examinations and Year Four
CHAPTER TEN
The Final Stretch
EPILOGUE
And Then, It All Made Sense
ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS
First and foremost, Alhamdulillah.
This journey would not have been possible without Allah’s mercy, protection, guidance, and the people He placed along my path.

To my parents, Mrs. Monsurat Onigbanjo and Mr. Muhammed Thanni Onigbanjo, thank you for your prayers, sacrifices, patience, and support throughout this journey. Thank you for standing by me through the good days and the difficult ones, and for believing in me even when I struggled to believe in myself. May Allah reward you abundantly and grant you goodness in this life and the Hereafter.

To my siblings and other members of the family, thank you for standing by me and supporting me in ways both big and small. Your encouragement, prayers, and sacrifices have been an important part of my story.

To my teachers, lecturers, supervisor, mentors, seniors, colleagues, friends, and classmates, thank you for every lesson, correction, word of encouragement, helping hand, and moment of support. Some of you may never realize how much your little acts meant to me, but I carry them with me.

To everyone who encouraged me to try again after every disappointment, prayed for me, checked on me, listened to me, guided me, helped me study, shared opportunities with me, or simply reminded me not to give up, thank you.
And to everyone who supported me in ways I may not even know about, Jazakumullahu khayran.
May Allah reward you abundantly, bless you, and make me a source of goodness to others, just as you have been a source of goodness to me. Ameen.
PROLOGUE
Before the Journey Began
Nine years later, I graduated.
And I did not just graduate. I finished with a FIRST CLASS HONOURS and three professional qualifications: RN, RM, and RPHN.
But none of this was planned exactly the way it eventually happened.
It was a combination of so many things. So many people. So many disappointments. So many attempts. So many prayers. So many moments when I had no idea what would happen next.
And somehow, it all clicked when I returned from university and my Dad reminded me of something I had almost forgotten. He reminded me of how much I used to struggle in science class.
Personally, I used to think my struggle began with my five UTME attempts. But the more I thought about it, the more I realised that it had started much earlier.
Maybe it started when I chose the science class in secondary school.
Maybe it started because I was too young to understand the importance of education at the time.
Or maybe, quite simply, books were hard, and I loved Disney, Zee World, and Nickelodeon too much.
Whatever the reason, the struggle was real.
And looking back now, I can see that every part of it was leading somewhere.

The remedial classes.The poor results.The five UTME attempts.The insults I endured.The IELTS examination.The applications.The disappointments.The unending clinical postings.The professional examinations.The leadership positions.
The falling CGPA.The tears.The prayers.The people Allah sent into my life.
Everything.
They all led me to this very moment.
CHAPTER ONE
MAYBE THE STRUGGLE STARTED EARLIER
When I think about my academic journey now, I realised that JAMB was not where the story started.
It started much earlier.
During my secondary school years, I struggled with science class.
Sometimes, I wondered, who even asked me to go for the sciences? Was it peer pressure, or did I genuinely think it would be a walk in the park? Lol.
I hated subjects like Mathematics, Chemistry, Physics, and Further Mathematics. Basically, anything that required me to calculate something was automatically my enemy.
I preferred subjects like Agricultural Science and Biology because they made more sense to me.
Agricultural Science was straightforward.
What is the advantage of crop rotation?
What is the disadvantage?
What is the importance of agriculture to humanity?
Simple.
Biology was different too. I could relate to it because it dealt with the human body and living things.
But Chemistry and Physics?
They looked like gibberish to me.
I had so many issues with the subjects I didn’t like. Looking back now, I remember being told that I performed woefully in some of my Chemistry and Mathematics examinations.
In fact, during my junior secondary school days, my class teacher, Mr Shoremekun, popularly known as Mr Show, enrolled me for remedial classes.
That should tell you something.
My struggle did not begin with JAMB.
It did not begin with university.
It started much earlier.
Maybe it started when I chose science class in secondary school.
Maybe I was simply too young to understand the importance of education at the time.
Or maybe, quite simply, BOOKS WERE HARD, and I loved Disney, Zee World, and Nickelodeon too much.
Whatever the reason, the struggle was real.
The only way out for me was not to “chop beans.”
In other words, I had to do everything within my power not to have an F in my results.
I wasn’t necessarily trying to become the best student in the school. Nah! Those positions were for the smart kids.
I was trying to survive.
And somehow, I survived.
I attended Lagos State Model College, Badore. When our set graduated in 2017, we didn’t even have a valedictory service because, apparently, our set was considered a notorious set.
Although, honestly, I think every graduating set is eventually called notorious.
But after leaving the school gate for the last time, I was faced with my own reality.
I was done with secondary school.
The SSCE was over.
There was no more classroom to hide in. No more teacher to remind me to read. No more school timetable telling me what to do.
I had to find my own way.
And that was when reality dawned on me.
I realised that I could no longer simply survive. I had to figure out what came next.
Luckily, I didn’t have to return to that school compound because we were done with our SSCE.
There was only one major thing left.
JAMB.
And that was where another chapter of the struggle began.
CHAPTER TWO
WHEN LIFE DIDN’T GO AS PLANNED
I took my first-ever UTME and scored 180. In my head, I thought, “Uhn. No worries. There’s still time. I can try again next year.”
I guess I was just trying to reassure myself then.
Interestingly, this was also the period when Heavenly Aura Spa, my brand, was birthed.

Again, during my secondary school days, my elder brother and I attended L.E.A.R.N. (Lagos Empowerment and Resource Network), where I learnt catering, bead making, and wirework. The third skill I acquired was makeup and tying of headwrap (gele), which was also the last time I attended L.E.A.R.N.

I had the rare opportunity of attending the programme three times, and although it was a great opportunity, it was my last skill-acquisition class that led me to discover my passion for the beauty industry.

I remember there was a competition in secondary school, and I volunteered to tie the gele for all the participants. My gele came out really nice, and from then on, I had it in mind to sharpen my skills.

Then my Mum introduced me to ELEGANT TWINS INSTITUTE OF COSMETOLOGY. She went there to inquire about the programme and told me that when she was much younger, she used to admire the beautiful women who attended the school. She suggested that I attend Elegant Twins.
At Elegant Twins, I honed my skills in makeup, gele tying, and nail artistry.
Along the way,
I developed a deep interest in beauty therapy, which inspired me to expand my skills to include massage, facials, pedicures, body scrubs, and much more.
It took me about three years to complete the beauty therapy programme, which was supposed to take just nine months, because of my back-and-forth with JAMB. Nevertheless, in 2019, I finally finished.
I was really determined to wrap up that stage of my life that year, and I did.
Now, it was time for JAMB.
So, I was juggling between writing UTME examinations and learning a trade at Elegant Twins. I kept pushing. Like I used to say to myself back then, “Na German German.”
Then I took my second UTME.
This one was a lot.
I scored 198.
It was sufficient enough to secure admission, but it wasn’t enough to gain admission into the course of my choice. With that 198 JAMB score, I was offered Health Education.
And the question became, “What do you want to do with this course upon graduation?”
But in my head, I thought, “Admission is admission. Life will figure itself out.”
My Dad told me not to go.
All efforts to secure admission into universities in Lagos proved abortive
Funny how I was also gaining weight during this stage of my life. With all that was happening, you would think I was supposed to lose weight. Instead, I was adding more.
These might sound funny now, but they weren’t funny then.
Then my uncle, Uncle Ayo, suggested that I attend Adams College.
He had actually suggested it during my second UTME, but, because I didn’t really know my way around Oshodi then. I was advised not to go.
But when JAMB decided to JAMB me again, I was eventually told to give it a try.
Did I cry during this?
YES. PREMIUM TEARS. I CRIED MY EYES OUT.
But I had HOPE.
One thing I kept reminding myself, even before I attended Adams, was that no leaf falls without the knowledge of Allah.
That was comforting, at least with the little knowledge I had then about the storms of life.
That statement helped me move on
CHAPTER THREE
THE THIRD ATTEMPT: ADAMS COLLEGE
The day I set foot in Adams College was indeed a turning point in my life.
As I entered through the right side of the entrance, I saw a backdrop showcasing high-flying students who had scored over 300 in JAMB.
And I thought, “How is this even possible?”
Coming from someone who had struggled to get up to 200 in my previous JAMB exams, seeing people score 300 was a bit surprising.
I stepped into the class.
I remember vividly. It was Mr. Adams’ class. He was teaching us Physics then, and the topic was pressure. The way he explained the formula P = F/A was one for the books.

He used the Nigerian network system as an example. He explained how, if you wanted to watch a video and the network kept buffering and buffering, you would eventually get bored. I found that really interesting.
Then there was our English tutor, Mr. Jahoski, with his FUNNY GRAMMAR.
Mr. Amos taught us Biology. He taught us well. There were in-depth explanations of the plant and animal kingdoms. Those topics are wide, but Mr. Amos made sure he touched everything necessary.
Then there was Wachie.
Mr.  Wachie’s style of teaching was interesting.
He said something that stuck with me while I was preparing for JAMB, and it became instrumental during my university days.
According to him, “Few days to any exam I’m having, I’d just go and hide somewhere and read my eyes out.”
Little did he know that what he was describing is what we Gen Zs now refer to as LOCK-IN.
And that’s exactly what I did on campus.
Once I saw that exams were in a few days, I would just lock in. I would delete all my social media apps.
YES. All of them, except WhatsApp, because I needed to get updates from my class group chat regarding notes, exam venues, and other important information.
Another thing that made Adams College standout for me was the fact that we had monthly mock examinations. It was called DIET then.
So, imagine everything you had been taught throughout the month and the months before that. You would get tested on it just to see where you understood.
And I don’t think I ever scored up to 200 in any of the DIETs.
It was hard ooo. Very hard.
Especially that English.
But I kept pushing.

Then Mr. Adams had this beautiful tradition of coming to our class at the beginning of every month. He would use the letters of the month to inspire us, turning each month into a little lesson of its own.
For example, for the month of May, he would say:
M — Make hay while the sun shines.A — Attention.Y — Your willpower.
Things like this really inspired us.
And then it was time for me to write the UTME.
For the first time in my life, I finally scored over 200.
I had 232.
I was happy.
I was proud of myself.
It turned out that almost everything we were taught at Adams came out in the UTME. The way Mr. Adams treated past questions then, ehn!
Like, we literally ate and slept with our books.
But at Adams, it wasn’t about books alone.
Mr. Adams also instilled in us the importance of prayer. You just had to pray, whether you were a Muslim or a Christian.
He used to say, “Action without prayer is dead.”
Meaning, you have to work and pray.
He also said, “Work as if you’ve never prayed, and pray as if you’ve never worked.”
Those words stuck with me.
You know, it was during this period that I met some of the most wonderful individuals I have EVER come across in my life, many of whom I still keep in touch with to this day.

People like Sister Maryam Sikiru, Labeebah Adelakun, Adesina Maryam, Nurse Fatimah Sarumi, Khadeejah Ademola, RAD. Miftahudeen Odeyinka, Mr. Abdulmojeed Miftahudeen, Sakinnah Daramola, Kharimah Daramola, Safanah Dhikrullah, Afra’u Dhikrullah, Moshood Siddiq, Phram. Maryam Akinbami, Nr. Muhammed Gbadeghesin, Zayyad, Mrs. Fatimah Onibon-Bello, Abdulrahman Shelle, Rofiah Surajudeen, Sumayyah Gabadeen, Aisha Abudu, Mrs. Maryam Adewunmi, Mrs. Maryam Lawal among others.
One day, after one of our tutorial classes, I went to pray.
And I thought, “It’s 4 p.m., right? What am I doing outside?”
I usually went straight home. When I first resumed, I had no friends in Adams, so after class, I would pray and go home.
Then I met Sumayyah Gabadeen.
Sumayyah was like, “Roqeebah, there’s usually an usrah at the mosque after Salah on some days.”
I can’t remember the exact days anymore. I think it was Thursdays, or maybe Tuesdays.
In summary, she invited me to come for usrah.
And yes, I can never forget someone like Sumayyah because that was a turning point for me.
I began to realise that I wasn’t alone.
I saw that there were many people who had written JAMB more than once. Some had written it twice. Others had tried several times.
And then I thought, “Uhm. Roqeebah, you’re not alone.”
I started rubbing shoulders with the amazing people I met there.
Another highlight, and in some ways, another turning point, of staying in that masjid was what happened with my hijab.
After secondary school in 2017, I thought the ideal thing was simply to cover my hair with a turban..
Then sometime in 2019, when I got to Adams College, I sat in the masjid.
I was asked why I hadn’t prayed Salah yet.
It was Rofiah Surajudeen who asked me that question.
And I said, point-blank, “I wasn’t with my scarf.”
The next thing Rofiah said SHOOK ME.
“Why won’t you be with your scarf?”
She said it in Yoruba.
It felt like a stray bullet.
I was numb. I didn’t know what to say.
At the time, I genuinely didn’t think it was a big issue. I thought I had simply forgotten my scarf. That was all.
But a few weeks later, while I was getting dressed to resume at Adams, I sat in front of my mirror. I lowered my turban….
Meaning, I wrapped my scarf properly around my head and stepped out.
And since then, it has been like that.
Moving on.
I met an amazing set of people at Adams. People of timber and calibre. Muslims who changed the way I viewed life.
In fact, it was through Zayyad, whom I met at Adams College, that I was able to attend my first IVC camp, and I was glad I did.
Also, towards the exams at Adams, we had Success Du'a.
Meaning, we would pray for the success of our UTME examinations. It was usually done on Fridays, and it was anchored by Ibn Kathir and Br. Toheed Junaid on the Friday before our UTME exams.
Then, after my third UTME examination, I proceeded to write the Post-UTME.
But before then, my mum’s Big sister, Dr. (Mrs.) Mujidat Ekundayo Mosanya, advised that I pick Physiotherapy after I told her I wanted a course that was similar to beauty therapy.
Then I did my findings.
And I was like, “Yes. I’ve found the course. This is what I want.”
Then, after my third attempt, I sat for the Post-UTME.
And yes, this time around, I moved from LASU to UI.
I just knew that I had to studyyyyy.
Maybe that was one of the reasons why I had 232.
Then the day of my Post-UTME at UI arrived, and I developed a migraine.
Why did that happen?
I guess I was under a lot of pressure.
For one, the school I picked UI was a tough university to get into, and I was really bent on reading everything that was required of me.
Plus, a day before, we had to travel to Ibadan. We had to scout around with other Adamites, and it was really difficult for me to get enough rest.
So, on the morning of the exam, my head began to hurt really badly.
Then I started crying because, first, I had a tough paper-based examination to write, and my headache wasn’t helping matters.
I was given some medication and water.
I remember crying that morning. On the way to get paracetamol, I met two UI students who made sure I was a bit calm.
May Allah bless them.
After I took the medication, I sat for my paper-based examination.
And when the results came out, I had 48%!
I wasn’t even pained because of the result itself.
I was pained by the way the news was broken to me.
I was asleep when my mum came to tell me that Uncle Ayo had checked my grades and that I had scored 48%.
In my head, I was like, “They should have just allowed me to check it myself.”
But I guess it was out of great concern that he quickly checked it.
This was in 2019.
I got stuck.
My mum was sitting at the edge of my bed, thinking, “What are we going to do now?”
I was lost because, before you could even gain admission into UI, you needed to have at least 50% in their Post-UTME.
I was stuck.
I was lost.
I was devastated.
I was extremely sad.
Plus, I still had the migraine.
Then I flipped through my books to see just how obsessed I was with Physiotherapy.
I had even learnt the general anthem to keep myself happy and busy.
In my mind, it’s, “Physiotherapy or Nothing.”
I had written “Physiotherapist Roqeebah” on almost every corner of my tutorial book.
You can imagine how sad I felt not getting it.
Very sad.
Nevertheless, I kept moving.

That was when I decided to sit for my first-ever intentional examination: IELTS. My aunt, Dr. Ajoke Onigbanjo’s friend, Dr. Kariah, suggested that I attend Erudite Millennium in Omole phase 1. It was there that I met tutors like Mentor Mo and Mr. Martins, who taught me very well and helped me prepare for the examination.
I had considered taking the SAT, but I wasn't particularly interested because I it involved Mathematics, a subject I struggled with at the time.
So, I focused on IELTS, sat for the examination, and passed.
But the finances were way above our budget, so I had to forfeit it.
I had to let go of another examination.
Making five so far, right?
Three UTME examinations.
One Post-UTME.
One IELTS.
This was tough.
Mind you, I was also trying to wrap up my cosmetology school during this period.
It was DAUNTING.
But I give Allah all the glory.
CHAPTER FOUR
MY COVID SEASON AND MY 2ND RETURN TO ADAMS COLLEGE
After my IELTS exams and the total completion of my cosmetology school, I had to move back to Adams College for the second time, and that was my fourth UTME attempt.

After IVC that year, I was so determined to pass my UTME examination. I picked UNILORIN this time, with the hope that once I sat for the exam, got good grades, and did everything right, I would finally get admitted.
But life had other plans.
There was a total lockdown due to the COVID-19 pandemic that occurred that year.

After my JAMB lessons at Adams College in 2020, I sat for the UTME examination. When I heard the results were out, I was scared, I knew I had to inform (RAD), Ustadh Miftahudeen Odeyinka, who has been really instrumental to my growth, from my days at Adams College till today.

Ustadh Miftahudeen monitored my progress and ensured that while I was focused on university, He made sure I didn’t lose focus on other important aspects of my life. He was also instrumental to my going back to Madrasah. He informed me about Mumtiah Madrasah, where I started learning my Arabic studies.
Sometimes, he even went as far as rewarding me for my hard work in university. He would send me money while I was in school as a means of encouragement.
May Allah SWT bless him and be with him and his wonderful wife, Dr. Fatimah Adubiaro. She was the Best Graduating Student of her set, and she’s also an Ustadha with lots of Islamic knowledge.
During my university days, she was one of the people I admired. Anytime I lacked motivation, I’d just search up her name and keep reading about her until I got my motivation back.
May Allah SWT bless the both of them and make their children the coolness of their eyes.
Eventually, I gathered the courage to check my result.
And I saw that I got 257 in UTME.
I was surprised and grateful because my trajectory in UTME was just rising.
Four UTME attempts, and I kept getting better.
So I thought and I had this conviction that I would gain admission into UNILORIN.
Then COVID-19 happened!!.
We had to start preparing for our Post-UTME at Adams College online. I kept reading and motivating myself, telling myself: It’s Physiotherapy or Nothing.
After the COVID-19 lockdown, we resumed back to Adams College. After a few weeks at Adams, UNILORIN announced that they would be merging two sets together.
They also announced that they wouldn’t be writing Post-UTME that year.
So I gave it a deep thought.
They’d be merging two sets due to COVID, and there would also be no Post-UTME. I guessed it was probably due to the large number of applicants.
Hmmn.
Then I decided to hunt for a job.
Remember I said I’m a certified spa therapist?
So, I went ahead to look for spas around me that aligned with my values.
I saw Hennapalace. I applied, and I was told that their slot on the mainland was filled and that I should apply to their spa on the Island.
Then I prayed about it, and that’s how I saw that Modest Muslimah was hiring a spa therapist.
I cooked my application letter and sent it to them.
And I was asked to come for an interview.
LOL.
This season was funny.
You know I mentioned that I gained serious weight while I was searching for admission?
So, when I got there, my boss at the time thought I was one elderly woman, whereas I was just 19 years of age.
I found that funny.
I did my interview, and she said I’d get a feedback in seven days.
Which I did.
I resumed work in December 2020.
Then I held on to UNILORIN for a long time, thinking, “Oh, my admission is near.”
I worked at Modest Muslimah for six months while I was still holding on to hope for UNILORIN.
Then, when I noticed the admission was taking too long, my mum suggested that I pick another UTME form, just to be on the safe side.
Which was what we did.
We picked another UTME, while still waiting for UNILORIN’s admission.
Guess what?
UNILORIN announced that they had finished giving out admission, just a week before the 2021 JAMB.
I was also sad because I refreshed my portal severally to see if I had been given admission.
In fact, my Dad’s friend, Uncle TJ, also tried everything within his power to see that I got into Ilorin.
I waited.
I cried.
I hoped.
During the last ten days of Ramadan, on one of the odd nights, I remember I cried. I cried really hard. I was really vulnerable.
Because I was thinking, there’s no way out again.
I had endured lots of indirect insults and the direct ones.
For the third time, after submitting my resignation letter at Modest Muslimah Lounge, I went back to Adams College.
I didn’t even have time to process my thoughts.
Which was rare.
And then came my 5th UTME examination.
CHAPTER FIVE
5TH UTME EXAM: CAIRO UNIVERSITY VS. CRESCENT UNIVERSITY
My stay at Adams College this time around was just for a week.
Shocking, right?.
Why would I just arrive a week before JAMB to start my revision classes?
All the same, I summoned courage, and I read.
I tried to cover the little I could, and I went to sit for my 5th UTME examination.
And when the results came out,  I had 187.
Back to square one !
I remember sending the result to my mum, and as usual, she came to sit at the edge of my bed, asking, “What would we do now?”
Everyone got tired and fed up.
Including me.
I didn’t know what to do.
Then my mum confided in Mrs. Hamza, her very good colleague at work.
Then Mrs. Hamza suggested that her children, Sis. Fadilah and Mubarak Hamza, and I should try out Cairo University.
Which we did.
Hmmmm….
This season made me cry a lot.
We applied for Cairo University.
The process took a lot of effort and money from my mum. But her ultimate goal was to see that I got admitted into a university with the course of my choice.
Were we given admission?
Yes.
Was it the course of choice?
No!
The admission was sent to us in Arabic.
I remember it was Mubarak who sent mine to my mum.
And when my brother showed me, I was happy.
I remember going to the back of my house, looking at a very strong tree I used to admire, and shedding lots of tears.
I thanked Allah.

In fact, when I thought it was Cairo University that I’d be attending, I was extremely happy. I started following their page and monitoring their next academic session like any other fresher would, making lots of enquiries.
Only for the admission letter that was written in Arabic to be translated into English, and I saw:
COMPUTER SCIENCE.
Is this a joke?!
After hoping, crying, and wishing, I saw Computer Science.
The agent was like, when we get to Egypt, it would be changed to the course of choice.
Like, seriously?.
Something you can’t change here in Nigeria, what’s the assurance that when I travel to Egypt, you’d give me my choice of course?
All of us, myself, Mubarak, and Sis. Fadilah had to forfeit it.
Another one gone!.
Gosh.
Hmmn.
It’s well.
Despite the challenges, I would  listen to Mufti Menk, Yasmin Mogahed, and Nouman Ali Khan’s lectures on perseverance, on how to have faith in the midst of adversity, and so on.
I’d just listen to them from time to time and have HOPE.

As time went on, I began to see my struggles as a test from Allah rather than a punishment. I had heard somewhere that any trial that brings you closer to Allah is a test, and when I looked at my own journey, I began to understand my struggles differently.
Perhaps all these years of waiting, crying, praying, and hoping were not a punishment. Perhaps they were a means of bringing me closer to Allah.
And one thing I usually do is look up at the sky.
I just like it.
Especially at night.
I love to gaze at the moon.
Then my watchword was:
“Keep making efforts until certainty overtakes.”
Then, one random evening, my Dad just sent a link to me via WhatsApp which stated that ROSULA Crescent University chapter was giving scholarships to students who finished their SSCE in 2020 and 2021.
I knew I wasn’t eligible.
Because mine was in 2017.
But, as per “keep making efforts,” right?
That’s how I applied to Crescent University, Abeokuta.
If Crescent University didn’t work, maybe Fountain or Al-Hikmah University would.
So, that’s how I stepped into Crescent University and entered the Deputy Registrar’s office. After completing my interview, I was handed my admission letter!
That moment was funny.
It got me contemplating my journey.
Like, after I got my admission letter, I came home, observed my Istikhara, and after the prayer, I read that admission letter again.
I was shocked.
Just like that?
The admission I’ve been searching for all this while.
The admission that I developed migraines over.
The admission I endured lots of insults for.
The admission I hoped for.
The admission I prayed for.
It was now in my hands.
Also, I got to realize that Crescent University had been working on establishing Nursing programme for the five years I was at home.
So, it meant that all the back and forth I was going through
Allah just wanted me to wait for His plan for my life.
All the setbacks were part of Allah’s decree.
The process actually changed my perspective on life.
And I’m extremely grateful to everyone who was a part of it.
But the story isn’t over yet.
I feel like crying at this point.
Cos I’m having lots flashbacks!
CHAPTER SIX
GAINING ADMISSION INTO CRESCENT
The 4th of October 2021 was the day I stepped into Crescent University as a full-time undergraduate student.
I didn’t even have the time to heal from the hurdle of JAMB or the past five years. As soon as I got my admission letter, I started preparing for my undergraduate degree.
I got new shoes, a school bag, new clothes, mostly Ankara, and my corporate school wear.

I did not always feel brilliant.
I did not always feel capable.
There were moments when I questioned myself and wondered if I would ever make it here.
But I kept going.

So, if you are reading this as the average student who feels stuck, the student who has failed before, the student who thinks everyone else is smarter, or the student who has started to believe that perhaps your dreams are simply too big for you, I hope my story finds you.
I hope it reminds you that you do not have to have it all figured out from the beginning.
You do not have to be the brightest person in the room.
You do not have to know from your first day on Earth, that you are destined for greatness.
Sometimes, you just have to keep going.
Keep learning.
Keep trying.
Keep becoming.
Because where you are now is not necessarily where your story ends.
I hope my story reaches the person I wrote it for.
The ordinary student who feels stuck.
The one who thinks they are not enough.
The one who is wondering if their own story will ever make sense.
And when it finally does, I hope they too can look back and say:
And then, it all made sense.
To My Dear Struggling Students,
I understand that you may not understand what is going on right now. I get it. You might feel like your world is crumbling around you and that no one truly understands what you are going through.
But I am here to reassure you that you are not alone, and there is HOPE.

I want you to have the AUDACITY to dream again. I want you to BELIEVE  in yourself, even when everything around you is making you doubt yourself. I want you to have the COURAGE to keep going. And I want to give you the REASSURANCE that even when it feels like nothing is going right, there is still LIGHT at the end of the tunnel.
You can still become whoever you want to be.

Take this from me, someone who struggled to find her feet, someone who did not always believe she was capable, and someone who had her own fair share of disappointments, doubts, and difficult seasons.
If I could find my way here, then perhaps you can find yours too.
So, keep going!
Your current chapter is not the entirety of your story.
There is still so much ahead of you.
